items.prompt: What is a "role definition" in the sense this unit uses it?
choices: A concrete list of the specific skills, behaviors, or outcomes a hire genuinely needs to succeed in this role
The official job title and level listed on the offer letter, which interviewers use to set expectations
A general description of the company's culture and values that every candidate is expected to fit
The approved salary band for the position, which determines how senior the hire needs to be
items.explanation: A role definition is specifically about the concrete requirements this job needs — not the title, culture, or compensation, which don't help design an interview loop.
items.reference:
Role definition
📋 A concrete list of specific skills/behaviors/outcomes
🚫 Not a title, not culture, not comp
Why: only a specific list gives an interviewer something to design a test around.
items.learnMore:
What makes a role definition usable

A role definition is useless for interview design if it reads like a job-ad bullet ("strong communicator," "technically excellent") — those are adjectives, not tests. The unit's own example contrasts vague traits ("seems smart," "good communicator," "good judgment") with the concrete, checkable signals an interviewer can actually build an exercise around, like diagnosing a production incident from partial logs.

Common mistake

Treating the job title or the salary band as if it were the role definition — neither tells an interviewer what to actually test for.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does defining the role before interviewing matter?
choices: It's what makes it possible to design a loop that deliberately tests for what the role needs, instead of hoping a good overall impression happens to cover them
It's a formal legal requirement that applies across most companies' standard hiring processes everywhere
It guarantees the team will be able to make an offer to a strong candidate noticeably faster overall
It mainly removes the need for the panel to hold any kind of debrief conversation afterward at all
items.explanation: L1 frames role definition as the thing that makes deliberate, targeted testing possible — not a speed shortcut or a compliance checkbox.
items.reference:
Defining before interviewing
1️⃣ Write the role definition first
2️⃣ Design the loop to test it on purpose
Why: a loop built before the role is defined can only hope a good impression happens to cover what matters.
items.learnMore:
Why order matters

If interviewing starts before the role's real requirements are written down, there's nothing yet to deliberately map interview slots to — the panel ends up testing whatever topics feel natural in conversation, which tends to converge on general impression rather than the specific skills the job actually needs day to day.

The Scenario's rushed hire is exactly this failure: the loop ran before (or without) a clear signal list, so nothing specifically pointed any slot at incident-diagnosis skill, and it went untested by default rather than by decision.

Making the offer to the candidate even faster than the team already managed to do
Skipping the interview process for this candidate entirely, given the time pressure
Guaranteeing in advance that the candidate would turn out to be a bad hire
items.explanation: A role definition written first is what lets a team point specific slots at specific requirements — exactly the step the Scenario's rushed process skipped.

items.prompt: How does a "signal" relate to a "role definition"?
choices: A signal is the observable evidence that a specific requirement from the role definition was actually demonstrated
A signal replaces the need for writing out a role definition at all during the hiring process
A signal is simply a synonym for the role definition — the two terms describe the same thing
A signal is only something that becomes relevant after an offer has already been extended
items.explanation: The role definition states what's required; a signal is the concrete, observed evidence that a specific requirement was actually met.
items.reference:
Signal vs. requirement
📐 Requirement: what the role definition states
👁️ Signal: the observed evidence it was demonstrated
Why: a requirement without an observed signal is just an assumption.
items.learnMore:
Turning a requirement into a signal

A signal has to be something an interviewer actually watches happen — not something a candidate asserts about themselves, and not a general vibe. "Can explain a trade-off clearly to a non-technical stakeholder" only becomes a usable signal once an interviewer designs a moment in the loop where a candidate actually has to do that, and watches whether it lands.

Common mistake

Accepting a candidate's self-report ("I'm a great communicator") as if it were equivalent to actually observing the behavior.

The interviewer coming away with a general feeling that the candidate seemed articulate
A reference from a prior manager confirming that the candidate is generally friendly
items.explanation: A signal has to be a direct, observed demonstration of the specific requirement — not a self-report, a vague impression, or an unrelated trait.

items.prompt: What is a "signal" in this unit's hiring framework?

A red flag in a candidate's background that automatically disqualifies them from the role
The overall gut feeling an interviewer walks away with about a candidate's fit

items.explanation: A signal is concrete, checkable evidence tied to a specific requirement — not a general impression, a disqualifier, or a reference call.
items.reference:
What counts as a signal
✅ A specific, observed action tied to a defined requirement
🚫 Not a gut feeling, a disqualifier, or a reference call
Why: only directly observed evidence can be scored independently of a general impression.
items.learnMore:
Signals are specific on purpose

The unit draws a sharp line between a signal and everything that merely resembles one: confidence, years of experience, and a good overall feeling are all real things an interviewer might notice, but none of them is tied to a specific, predetermined requirement being demonstrated. A signal has to answer "what did I actually watch this candidate do," not "how did I feel about them."

items.prompt: What is the "halo effect"?
choices: The tendency for one salient positive trait to bias the perceived strength of other, unrelated traits
The tendency for interviewers to favor candidates who show up late to the interview
A scoring bonus the panel is instructed to give to internal employee referrals
The tendency for a candidate's actual skills to improve over an interview process
items.explanation: The halo effect is specifically about one trait unconsciously coloring judgment of unrelated traits — not about lateness, referrals, or actual skill improvement.
items.reference:
Halo effect
✨ One salient trait
🎭 ...unconsciously colors unrelated traits
Why: confidence in the Scenario became a stand-in for skills nobody actually tested.
items.learnMore:
A well-documented bias

The halo effect is a long-studied finding in psychology: once someone forms a strong positive (or negative) impression of one trait, that impression bleeds into how they judge other, unrelated traits — a classic study found that students rated as more physically attractive were also rated as more intelligent and more likely to succeed, with nothing about intelligence actually assessed.

In hiring, the dangerous version is a visible, easy-to-notice trait like confidence standing in for a harder-to-observe one, like technical judgment, that never actually got checked.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, which trait most plausibly triggered a halo effect across the panel?

The candidate's years of prior experience listed on their resume
The candidate's stated salary expectations going into the loop
items.explanation: Confidence and articulateness are the visible, salient traits described in the Scenario — the untested skill (incident diagnosis) is exactly what the halo effect caused the panel to assume without checking.

items.prompt: What distinguishes a "structured interview loop" from an unstructured one?
choices: Each interview slot is assigned to test a specific, predetermined signal, and interviewers score independently before comparing notes
A structured loop simply always has more total interview slots than an unstructured one
A structured loop is conducted entirely over video calls instead of meeting in person
A structured loop always takes place across multiple days rather than a single day
items.explanation: Structure is about what each slot deliberately tests and independent scoring — not about the number of slots, the medium, or the schedule.
items.reference:
Structured loop
🎯 Each slot tests one predetermined signal
🔒 Interviewers score independently, before comparing notes
Why: structure is about what's tested and when scores are shared — not slot count or format.
items.learnMore:
What structure actually buys you

Two loops can have the identical number of interviews, in the identical format (video, in-person, whatever), and still differ completely in whether they're structured — the difference is entirely in whether each slot is assigned a specific, predetermined thing to test, and whether interviewers commit to a score before hearing anyone else's impression.

Common mistake

Assuming more interviews automatically means more coverage. Five unstructured conversations can test the exact same thing five times over.

The gap wasn't dishonesty or laziness; it was the absence of a role definition and a structured loop to test against it, which let a salient trait quietly substitute for the one skill that actually mattered.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, if five interviewers all rate a candidate highly based on the same salient trait, how many independent data points does that actually represent?
choices: Effectively one — all five ratings trace back to the same single trait, not five separately-tested skills
Five — agreement across five interviewers always means five genuinely independent data points
Zero — per L2, agreement across a panel of interviewers is never meaningful at all

items.explanation: L2's diagram shows every interviewer's positive impression tracing back to the same source trait — that's one signal repeated, not five independent ones.
items.reference:
One trait, five votes
🙂 Candidate is confident
➡️ All 5 interviewers trace back to that one trait
Why: agreement is only meaningful if each interviewer tested something distinct.
items.learnMore:
Why consensus can be an illusion

Five people agreeing feels like strong evidence, because in most contexts independent agreement is strong evidence. The catch is the word "independent" — if all five arrived at their rating by noticing the same visible trait rather than testing five separate things, the panel has produced one data point wearing five people's signatures, not five real checks.

This is also why the unit is careful to say confidence itself isn't the problem — a confident candidate can also be genuinely skilled. The problem is using confidence as a substitute for checking the skill directly.

A different role — sales, design, support — needs its own list, built by asking the same question for that job specifically: what would someone actually have to do, in front of an interviewer, to prove this is true?

items.prompt: Per L2, once signals are defined, what changes about how each interview slot is used?

Every slot simply becomes a general open-ended conversation, just extended to run longer

items.explanation: The core design move is mapping distinct signals to distinct slots with independent scoring — not lengthening or eliminating conversations.
items.reference:
Slots follow signals
📝 Signal defined first
🎯 Slot assigned to test exactly that signal, scored independently
Why: the loop is built around the signals — not the other way around.
items.learnMore:
Independent scoring is the second half of the mechanism

Mapping a signal to a slot only does half the work — the other half is making sure each interviewer commits their own score before hearing anyone else's take. Skip that second half and a confident early interviewer's enthusiasm can anchor the rest of the panel regardless of what their own slot actually tested, quietly recreating the halo effect inside a loop that looks structured on paper.

Five such interviews don't give five times the coverage — they give one measurement, repeated, dressed up as five independent opinions.

items.prompt: Per L2, what actually determines what each interview slot tests?
choices: The specific signals identified in the role definition — the loop is designed around them, not the other way around
Whichever topics the interviewer running that particular slot personally finds most interesting
The order in which candidates happen to be scheduled to interview during the week

items.explanation: L2's loop-design section is explicit: signals come from the role definition first, and slots get built around them — not the reverse.
items.reference:
Which comes first
1️⃣ Role definition (the signals)
2️⃣ Loop design (slots mapped to those signals)
Why: there's nothing to deliberately map slots to until the signals already exist.
items.learnMore:
Designing backwards from a vague loop doesn't work

It might seem possible to design the interview slots first and figure out what they tested afterward, but that reverses the only part of the process that actually prevents the halo effect: deliberately deciding, in advance, what each slot is for. Without that order, slots default to open-ended conversation, and the role definition — if it gets written at all — ends up describing what happened to get tested rather than what the role actually needs.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, why is "can independently diagnose a production incident from partial, ambiguous information" usable in an interview while "technically strong" is not?

items.reference:
Buildable vs. not
✅ "Identify which of 3 fixes addresses the root cause" — a real 45-min exercise
❌ "Good judgment" — no exercise to build
Why: a concrete task converts directly into an exercise; an adjective doesn't.
items.learnMore:
The test an interviewer can actually run

A useful way to check whether a signal is specific enough: could a different interviewer, who's never met this candidate, sit down and build a concrete exercise from the sentence alone? "Can identify which of three proposed fixes addresses the root cause" passes that test — you can picture the exercise immediately. "Has good judgment" doesn't; it leaves the interviewer to invent their own definition of judgment on the spot, which is exactly how the halo effect sneaks back in.

Specific doesn't mean negative

items.explanation: L3 is explicit that a role's real requirements shift over time — a role definition written once and left alone drifts out of sync with what actually matters now.
items.reference:
Role definitions go stale
📜 Written once, never revisited
⏳ Tests for what used to matter
Why: a role's real requirements shift as the team or product changes.
items.learnMore:
A living document, not a one-off artifact

A role definition is a snapshot of what a job needs right now — written a year ago for a team that has since changed its stack, its scope, or its stage of growth, it can keep testing for signals that no longer matter while missing new ones that do. Treating it as something to revisit periodically (alongside the loop built on it) is what keeps it actually describing the job being hired for.

💬 Vague impression → nothing concrete to weigh
